title: Walking Is How I Think. On Routes, Loops, and Ideas That Arrive Mid-Step
body: I do not solve problems at desks. I walk them. This is not a fitness claim and it is not romantic. It is closer to a technical observation about where my own thoughts come from. At a desk, a hard problem presents itself like a wall. Everything at once, nothing movable. Somewhere in the second kilometer of a walk, the same problem presents itself like a corridor. There is a direction to it. There are doors. I am not the first to notice this. Walkers have been saying it for centuries, and thinkers who claimed otherwise often turn out, on inspection, to have been walkers too. But you do not need the lineage. You need one week of walking the same route and watching what your mind does with the material you feed it. The same route matters more than most people believe. New scenery is a gift, but it is also a tax. Every unfamiliar street charges attention, and attention is the thing a thinking walk is supposed to free. The known route asks nothing. The feet manage it. And whatever the mind was too busy to process in the morning shows up, unbidden, somewhere around the bend with the broken fence. There is a phase to it, and knowing the phases keeps me patient. The first twenty minutes are loud. The day replays itself, conversations negotiate their better endings, the mind fetches anxieties like a dog bringing sticks. I have learned to let the fetch happen. The noise burns off like morning fog, and it burns off only if you keep moving. The second phase is quiet, and it feels like nothing. This is the phase people quit in, walking back with nothing to show. But the quiet is the workshop, not the waiting room. Something is being rearranged in there. The evidence arrives later, mid-shower, mid-dish, mid-sentence, when the idea that was missing walks in wearing no label at all. The third phase is the arrival. It almost never comes as a conclusion. It comes as a question that finally has a shape, or as a sentence that suddenly knows where it is going. I carry no notebook, because stopping to write breaks the gait, and the gait is the engine. What I have noticed is that a true arrival survives the walk home. A false one does not. By the time the door is in sight, I know which ideas were buildings and which were scaffolding, because only the buildings are still standing. None of this requires mountains. The loop around ordinary blocks will do. Weather helps and hinders in equal measure; rain empties the streets and sharpens the quiet. What matters is the duration past the noise and the repetition past the boredom, because boredom, it turns out, is not the opposite of thinking. It is the price of admission. The desks won in the end, of course. The world now meets through screens, and the walking hours look, from the outside, like unaccounted time. But every serious thing I have ever worked out was worked out between streetlights, moving at the speed a body was built for, thinking at the speed a mind can keep. So here is my quiet proposal for anyone carrying a heavy question this week. Take it for a walk. The same three blocks, past the same broken fence, long enough for the noise to burn off. And when the idea arrives, mid-step, unlabeled, in the third kilometer or the third week. Where will you notice it first?
